==English== {{root|en|ine-pro|*new- (nod)}} ===Pronunciation=== * {{enPR|nēd|a=RP}}, {{IPA|en|/niːd/|[nɪi̯d]}} * {{IPA|en|/nid/|a=GA,CA}} * {{audio|en|En-us-need.ogg|a=GA}} * {{audio|en|LL-Q1860 (eng)-Vealhurl-need.wav|a=Southern England}} * {{homophones|en|knead|kneed}} * {{rhymes|en|iːd|s=1}} ===Etymology 1=== {{ety|en|:inh|enm:nede|id=noun|tree=1}} From {{inh|en|enm|nede}}, a merger of two terms: * {{inh|en|ang|nīed}} (West Saxon), {{m|ang|nēd}} (Mercian), {{m|ang|nēad|t=necessity, compulsion, want}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*naudi}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*naudiz}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*neh₂w-|t=death}}. * {{inh|en|ang|nēod|t=desire, longing}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*niudi|t=desire, eagerness}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*new-||to incline, tend, move, push, nod, wave}}. ====Noun==== {{en-noun|~}} # {{lb|en|countable|and|uncountable}} A {{l|en|requirement}} for something; something {{l|en|needed}}. #: {{syn|en|occasion|use}} #: {{ux|en|There's no '''need''' to speculate; we can easily find out for sure.}} #: {{ux|en|The retreat filled his '''need''' for solitude.}} #: {{ux|en|She grew irritated with his constant '''need''' for attention.}} #: {{ux|en|Our instant '''needs''' are not being met.}} #: {{ux|en|I've always tried to have few '''needs''' beyond food, clothing and shelter.}} #* {{RQ:Shakespeare Richard 2|act=IV|scene=i|passage=Being so great, I have no '''need''' to beg.}} #* {{RQ:Taylor Holy Living|passage=Be governed by your '''needs''', not by your fancy.}} #* {{RQ:Economist|date=2014-06-14|volume=411|issue=8891 |title=[http://www.economist.com/news/science-and-technology/21604091-it-possible-sniff-out-problems-sewer-pipes-they-happen-its-gas It's a gas] |passage=One of the hidden glories of Victorian engineering is proper drains.{{...}}But out of sight is out of mind. And that, together with the inherent yuckiness of the subject, means that many old sewers have been neglected and are in dire '''need''' of repair.}} # A [[desire]] or [[craving]] for the [[satisfaction]] of a requirement perceived as [[essential]] or [[primal]]. # Lack of means of subsistence; [[poverty]]; [[indigence]]; [[destitution]]. #* {{RQ:Shakespeare Romeo and Juliet|act=V|scene=i|passage=Famine is in thy cheeks;
'''Need''' and oppression starveth in thine eyes.}} =====Derived terms===== {{col|en|needly|needsome|needways|needwise|preneed |a friend in need is a friend indeed |if need be|need more time in the also==== * [[in need]] ===Etymology 2=== {{ety|en|:inh|enm:neden|id=verb|tree=1}} From {{inh|en|enm|neden}}, from {{inh|en|ang|nēodian}}. ====Verb==== {{en-verb}} # {{lb|en|transitive}} To have an absolute requirement for. #: {{ux|en|Living things '''need''' water to survive.}} #: {{ux|en|You do not always '''need ''' to go to the library to study. You may use the Internet.}} #: {{ux|en|She '''need'''ed convincing that I was what she really '''need'''ed.}} # {{lb|en|transitive}} To want strongly; to feel that one must have something. #: {{ux|en|After ten days of hiking, I '''needed''' a shower and a shave.}} # {{lb|en|modal|chiefly in the negative and interrogative}} To be obliged or required (to do something). #: {{ux|en|I '''need''' not go if I don't want to, '''need''' I?}} #: {{ux|en|I was wondering if I '''need''' fill in more forms. - No, that's the only one you '''need''' fill out.}} #: {{ux|en|I '''need''' never have packed my set of sunglasses - it rained all day every day.}} # {{lb|en|intransitive}} To be required; to be necessary. #* {{RQ:Locke Human Understanding|21|143|edition=2nd|text=When we have done it, we have done our duty, and all that is in our power, and indeed all that '''needs'''.}} #* {{quote-journal|en|date=2013-06-28|author=w:Joris Luyendijk| volume=189| issue=3| page=21| magazine=w:The Guardian Weekly| title=[http://www.guardian.co.uk/commentisfree/joris-luyendijk-banking-blog/2013/jun/19/banking-britain-beyond-control Our banks are out of control]| passage=Seeing the British establishment struggle with the financial sector is like watching an alcoholic who still resists the idea that something drastic '''needs''' to happen for him to turn his life around.}} # {{lb|en|obsolete|transitive}} To be [[necessary]] (to someone). #* {{RQ:Spenser Faerie Queene|book=II|canto=IX|passage=More ample spirit, then hitherto was wount, / Here '''needes''' me {{...}}}} =====Usage notes===== * The verb {{m|en||need}} is construed in a few different ways: ** With a direct object, as in “I need your help.” ** With a ''to''-infinitive, as in “I need to go.” Here, the subject of {{m|en||need}} serves implicitly as the subject of the infinitive. ** With a clause of the form “for [object] to [verb phrase]”, or simply “[object] to [verb phrase]” as in “I need for this to happen” or “I need this to happen.” In both variants, the object serves as the subject of the infinitive. ** As a modal verb, with a bare infinitive; in negative polarity contexts, such as questions (“Need I say more?” “Need you have paid so much?”), with negative expressions such as {{m|en|not}} (“It need not happen today”; “No one need ever know”), and with similar constructions (“There need only be one”; “it need be signed only by the president”; “I need hardly explain it”). {{m|en||Need}} in this use does not have inflected forms, apart from the contraction {{m|en|needn't|needn’t}}. ** With a gerund-participle, as in “The car needs washing”, or, in some North American dialects, with a past participle, as in “The car needs washed”"[https://ygdp.yale.edu/phenomena/needs-washed Needs washed]" by Zach Maher and Jim Wood, ''Yale Grammatical Diversity Project: English in North America'', 2011 (both meaning roughly “The car needs to be washed”). ** With a direct object and a predicative complement, as in “We need everyone here on time” (meaning roughly “We need everyone to be here on time”) or “I need it gone” (meaning roughly “I need it to be gone”). ** In certain dialects, and colloquially in certain others, with an unmarked reflexive pronoun, as in “I need me a car.” * A sentence such as “I need you to sit down” or “you need to sit down” is more polite than the bare command “sit down”, but less polite than “please sit down”. It is considered somewhat condescending and infantilizing, hence dubbed by some “the kindergarten imperative”, but is quite common in American usage.“[http://www.slate.com/id/2145734 You Need To Read This: How need to vanquished have to, must, and should.]” by Ben Yagoda, Slate, July 17, 2006 =====Conjugation===== {{en-conj|old=1}} =====Synonyms===== * {{sense|desire}} {{l|en|desire}},
